name: Cryptic crossword No 26,276
preamble: Nine of the across solutions are of a kind, not further defined

clue.text: An idiot

blocks.note: taken as written
a twerp is a silly, annoying person

explanation.walkthrough: The preamble says nine acrosses are of one kind and left undefined: they are all ports, so the whole clue here is wordplay. Antwerp is the great Belgian port.
explanation.definitionFit: Antwerp in Belgium is one of Europe's busiest seaports, so it belongs to the preamble's unnamed set of harbour towns.

clue.text: Essentially, one got the lot, each of whom little expected

definitions.note: completes 'one ... of whom little (is) expected', a noun phrase; 'one' does double duty

indicators.note: the essence of a thing is its core, so only the central letters are kept

blocks.note: the central letter of each of the four words
per means each, as in 'a pound per person'

explanation.surface: A lottery winner who, like every other winner, never dreamed of the jackpot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One got the lot' sounds like a jackpot win, but it is just four words whose middle letters are wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-hoper is a person with no prospect of success, someone nobody expects much from.

clue.text: Drew a dicky bird

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for weak or unsound, so the letters are in poor order and get rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sketched a little bird; 'dicky bird' is nursery talk for any small bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky bird' reads as one phrase, but 'dicky' (shaky, unsound) is the anagram signal and 'bird' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Waders are long-legged shore birds such as herons, curlews and sandpipers that feed in shallow water.

clue.text: Said perhaps to follow music link

indicators.note: to follow is to come after, so this piece is placed second

blocks.note: rap is a style of music
Port Said in Egypt is an example of a port, signalled by 'perhaps'

explanation.surface: A spoken suggestion that a musical connection should come next.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Said' looks like a verb but is Port Said, the Egyptian harbour at the Suez Canal; 'perhaps' marks it as one example of a port.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapport is a close, sympathetic connection between people, a bond or relationship of understanding.

clue.text: What's in the toilet? A note

indicators.note: something that is in another thing sits within it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: lav is short for lavatory
'eh?' is a way of saying 'what?'
re is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about something found in the lavatory, answered by a scrap of paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark makes it look like a riddle; read the 's as 'is'. Lav is British slang for a toilet, and Le Havre is the French port at the mouth of the Seine.
explanation.definitionFit: Le Havre is a major French seaport on the Channel coast, one of the preamble's unnamed set of harbour towns.

clue.text: Substitute saxophone for bass tuba; get jazz at last!

indicators.note: 'at last' points to the end of each word, so only final letters are kept

blocks.clueFragment: saxophone for bass tuba; get jazz
blocks.note: the final letter of each of these six words

explanation.surface: A bandleader's advice: swap the tuba for a sax and you'll finally be playing jazz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Substitute' looks like an instruction to swap instruments, but it is the definition; the six words after it only supply their last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz, from German, describes an inferior imitation used in place of the real thing, an adjective for a replacement.

clue.text: Decoration makes a point about sailors?

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: taken as written
a dot is a small point
RN is the Royal Navy, and its sailors are its men

explanation.surface: A medal is pinned on, raising the question of whether it points at seamen.
explanation.walkthrough: RN is the standard abbreviation for the Royal Navy, Britain's navy; 'sailors' here becomes RN MEN, and DOT goes round them.
explanation.definitionFit: An adornment is an ornament or embellishment added to make something look more attractive.

clue.text: Side roads where deserter is true to type

blocks.note: a rat is someone who deserts a cause, as rats leave a sinking ship
from the idiom 'runs true to type', where runs means is

explanation.surface: Back streets where a turncoat behaves exactly as you'd expect.
explanation.walkthrough: A rat run is British slang for a minor road drivers use as a shortcut to dodge traffic; the second piece comes from the phrase 'runs true to type'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rat runs are minor residential streets used by commuters as shortcuts to avoid congested main roads.

clue.text: Sets the speed at which cool current is flowing

definitions.note: a verb phrase describing what the device does; the answer is a noun

indicators.note: something flowing is fluid and on the move, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A thermostat or river gauge fixing the rate at which a chilled stream runs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all about water flow, but 'current' is only fodder; the definition describes a car feature.
explanation.definitionFit: Cruise control is a car system that holds the vehicle at a speed chosen by the driver without the accelerator.

clue.text: My colleague's cast

definitions.note: a proper name: Shed is a fellow Guardian setter

blocks.note: first meaning: the Guardian crossword setter who uses this pseudonym, a colleague of Philistine
second meaning: to throw off, as a snake does its skin

explanation.walkthrough: The setter speaks in her own voice: 'my colleague' is another Guardian setter, known by that pseudonym. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A snake or tree that casts its skin or leaves is said to drop them off, the verb sense of the word.

clue.text: Recurrent bad mood, say

indicators.note: a current that runs back on itself flows the other way, so these letters run backwards

blocks.note: a strop is a fit of bad temper
to mouth words is to say them

explanation.surface: Someone with a habitually sulky temperament, for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recurrent' looks like an adjective for the mood but is the signal to turn STROP round. Portsmouth is the English naval port on the south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Portsmouth, home of the Royal Navy on England's south coast, is a busy harbour city and one of the preamble's set.

clue.text: As an alternative to work taking precedence

indicators.note: to take precedence is to come first, so this piece is placed at the front

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a musical work
'or' offers an alternative, followed by 'to' as written

explanation.surface: Choosing something else rather than letting the job come first.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'OR TO' then 'OP', but OP takes precedence and goes in front. Oporto is the English name for Porto, Portugal's port-wine city.
explanation.definitionFit: Oporto, also called Porto, is a seaport city in northern Portugal, giving its name to port wine and joining the preamble's set.

clue.text: Joining EU may be unsuitable

indicators.note: 'may be' offers a possible rearrangement, so the letters can be reordered into something else
the answer joined to a piece makes up the shuffled word, so that piece must be taken away again

blocks.note: the whole word is the fodder
the European Union, removed from the rearranged letters

explanation.surface: A politician's warning that Turkey's entry to the European Union might be a bad fit.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus EU rearranges to 'unsuitable'. The surface nods to Turkey's long bid to join the EU, Istanbul being its great port.
explanation.definitionFit: Istanbul on the Bosphorus is Turkey's largest city and principal seaport, so it fits the preamble's unnamed set.

clue.text: Not having the bottle for faster moves in bed

indicators.note: whatever moves changes position, so the letters are rearranged
'in' places one thing inside another

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written
taken as written; it wraps around the rearranged letters

explanation.surface: Someone lacking the nerve for quicker action between the sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not having the bottle' reads as lacking courage (British slang 'bottle'), but here it means a baby not given a feeding bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby fed at the mother's chest rather than from a feeding bottle went without bottle milk, the literal sense.

clue.text: Maids wiggling coxae halfway to 23

indicators.note: wiggling means twisting about, so the letters move into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written
coxa is the anatomical Latin for the hip; coxae is its plural

explanation.surface: Young women swinging their hips, with an odd cross-reference tacked on.
explanation.walkthrough: 23 is BOWSPRIT, the spar at a ship's front, so halfway to it is the middle of the vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Amidships means in the middle part of a ship, midway between bow and stern, so halfway along towards the front spar.

clue.text: Three showing restraint

blocks.note: first meaning: a hunting term for a set of three hounds, hares or birds
second meaning: a lead for holding a dog

explanation.walkthrough: The obscure sense is a hunting word: a set of three animals, originally three hounds held on one lead.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog's lead holds it back, and in old hunting language a trio of hounds or game was counted by that name.

clue.text: Part

blocks.note: first meaning: to divide or separate, as a verb
second meaning, supplied by the preamble: the Croatian port on the Adriatic

explanation.walkthrough: The one clue word gives the verb meaning; the preamble's undefined category supplies the other, the port of Split on Croatia's Dalmatian coast.
explanation.definitionFit: To part things is to divide them, and the Croatian harbour city on the Adriatic shares that spelling.

clue.text: Apprentice finds postgraduate education starts to contain mindless repetition

indicators.note: starts are beginnings, so only the opening letter of each word is kept
to contain is to hold within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: the first letters of the three words
learning by rote is learning by repetition without understanding

explanation.surface: A trainee discovers that graduate study begins with parrot-learning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts' covers all three words of 'postgraduate education', not just one; the result wraps around the rote learning.
explanation.definitionFit: A protégé is a person guided and supported by an older mentor, much as a trainee learns a trade from a master.

clue.text: Frequently at the bottom

blocks.note: lowest means at the bottom
oft is an old word for often

explanation.surface: Something that keeps ending up at the very bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are written in the reverse of the clue's order. Lowestoft is a fishing port in Suffolk, the most easterly town in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Lowestoft is a Suffolk harbour town on England's east coast, historically a herring fishing port, so it joins the preamble's set.

clue.text: Demanding information on the way out?

indicators.note: 'on' here means placed upon and set into, so one piece is lodged within the other

blocks.note: an exit is a way out
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Someone insisting on directions as they leave the building.
explanation.walkthrough: Gen is informal British for information, as in 'get the gen'. It is lodged inside the way out.
explanation.definitionFit: Exigent describes something pressing or requiring much, an urgent or exacting situation or person.

clue.text: Cremation or perhaps burial, if fuel ran out

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Without fuel for the furnace, the body might have to be buried instead of burned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran out' reads as a phrase, but 'ran' is fodder and 'out' alone is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A funeral is the ceremony of laying a dead person to rest, whether by cremation or by burial, each an example.

clue.text: Can scientific leader probe the cause of mad cow disease?

indicators.note: a leader goes at the front, so only the opening letter is kept
to probe is to push into something, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.clueFragment: the cause of mad cow disease
blocks.note: a prion is the misfolded protein behind BSE
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A question of whether a top scientist is able to investigate BSE.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' opens the question as a verb but is the definition: can is slang for jail. Prions are the infectious proteins that cause BSE.
explanation.definitionFit: In American and British slang, the can is a jail, a place where convicts are locked up.

clue.text: Pole, tie and skewer? That's about right

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: a bow is a knot or bow tie
a spit is a rod for roasting meat
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A list of long thin objects, with someone confirming it is about correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's about right' reads as an approving remark, but 'about' is a containment signal acting on the skewer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowsprit is the spar projecting forward from a sailing ship's front, a nautical example of a long pole.

clue.text: I find that's god inside

indicators.note: inside means within, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: i.e. is short for id est, 'that is'
Odin is the chief Norse god

explanation.surface: A personal declaration that the divine is within.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' looks like the speaker, but it is the definition: I is the chemical symbol of this element.
explanation.definitionFit: I is the chemical symbol for iodine, the element with atomic number 53.

clue.text: On the way back, got drunk and opted for redevelopment in the station

indicators.note: travelling back means going the opposite direction, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: to tope is to drink heavily; toped is the past tense
a second, confirming route: these five letters rearranged give the same answer, so no letters are added

explanation.surface: Returning home after drinks, someone voted for rebuilding the railway station.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue offers a second route to the same five letters: 'opted for redevelopment' is an anagram of 'opted', confirming the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: A depot is a bus or railway terminus, especially in American usage, as well as a storage place for vehicles.

clue.text: Two struggling with sex life

indicators.note: struggling means twisting and writhing, so the letters move into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A couple having difficulties in the bedroom.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is wordplay. Felixstowe in Suffolk is Britain's busiest container port.
explanation.definitionFit: Felixstowe on the Suffolk coast handles more container traffic than anywhere else in Britain, so it joins the preamble's set.

clue.text: Somewhat disproportionate

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only some of the following word is used

blocks.note: the letters run inside this word

explanation.walkthrough: The undefined theme word turns out to be the theme itself: the answer is the generic word for the category the preamble means.
explanation.definitionFit: The other undefined acrosses are all harbour towns, and this entry is simply the general word for such a harbour.

clue.text: Marine lads or "salts"

definitions.note: a verb, third person: adds flavour to

blocks.note: marine means of the sea
sons are lads, male children

explanation.surface: Young seamen, otherwise known as old salts.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks push 'salts' towards its noun sense of old sailors, but it is a verb meaning flavours food.
explanation.definitionFit: A cook who salts a dish flavours it, and to season food is to add salt, pepper or spices.

clue.text: Now see gallery in artful style at work that's grand

indicators.note: 'in' places one thing inside another

blocks.note: artful means cunning or sly
the Tate is the London art gallery
a second, confirming route: the first two words rearranged give the same answer, so no letters are added

explanation.surface: An invitation to visit a gallery showing clever, impressive work.
explanation.walkthrough: A second route gives the same answer: 'style at work' is an anagram of 'style at'. The Tate is a group of London galleries.
explanation.definitionFit: Stately means dignified and imposing, the quality of a grand country house or a grand procession.
